description: Bush Coding is a solo team from Costa Rica, participating virtually from the San José Local Event. I'm a software developer and university student (UTN) focused on web development, data visualization and AI. I'm tackling wildfire and agricultural burning, a real problem in Central and Latin America, by turning NASA satellite fire data into a clear, consistent tool for emergency responders.
summary: EmberCal is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for Central America. NASA's two fire sensors, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), count fires very differently: VIIRS sees about five times more hotspots, and early MODIS years had only one satellite. Stitched together naively, the record shows fake jumps. EmberCal harmonizes both sensors with a method we validated on six years of data it never saw, cutting the typical error from 75% to 30%. Fire managers can pick a country, draw a box, or search around a point, and see which months and years burned most, how this month compares with its history, the active fires of the last 7 days, and when the next critical fire period starts. Everything can be downloaded as CSV or PNG and shared with a link. Fires and agricultural burning are a growing problem in Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica; EmberCal gives local responders a long, reliable baseline to anticipate the critical season.
details:
What it does

EmberCal answers three questions for any area of Central America: when does it burn, which years were extreme, and is this month normal?

  • Area selection: all seven countries, one country, a box drawn on the map, a point and radius (typed or clicked on the map), or coordinates; any month range from January 2001 to November 2026.
  • Burning calendar: a years by months grid colored by the number of hotspots, with an accessible single-hue color ramp.
  • Compared with normal: each month against the median of the same month across all years, on a blue, gray and red scale.
  • What is happening now: active fires of the last 7 days on the map and counted in the selected area, and the current month on pace against a typical month (with its percentile).
  • Fire season outlook: the critical period of the selected area, the share of the year's fire it holds and how many weeks until it starts, to plan patrols and burn permits ahead.
  • Seasonal profile (median month and typical range) and a year-by-year chart.
  • Downloads and sharing: the calendar and every hotspot as CSV, the calendar and charts as PNG images, and a link that keeps the selected view.
  • A Method page that explains the harmonization, the blind test and the accessibility choices.

How the harmonization works

  1. Same definition of a fire: only presumed vegetation fires (type 0); low-confidence detections removed in both sensors.
  2. Same pixel size: VIIRS pixels are 375 m and MODIS about 1 km, so one fire lights several VIIRS pixels. VIIRS detections in the same ~1 km cell during the same overpass are counted once (removes 26% of VIIRS detections).
  3. Same number of satellites: before July 2002 MODIS flew only on Terra. Using 2003-2019, when Terra and Aqua both flew, we learned the Terra+Aqua / Terra ratio for each month of the year and scaled Nov 2000-Jun 2002.
  4. Calibration where both sensors overlap (2012-2025): the VIIRS-1km / MODIS ratio is estimated for every 1° × 1° area and month of the year, with statistical shrinkage toward the area average and the regional monthly value when data are scarce, keeping regional totals equal to what VIIRS measured.
  5. One series: measured VIIRS from 2012, calibrated MODIS before. When the S-NPP near-real-time feed stopped on 2 November 2026, EmberCal continued with VIIRS on NOAA-20, scaled by the ratio measured on the days both observed. The method is ready for the next sensor change.

Validation (blind test)

Ratios calibrated only with 2012-2019 were used to predict, from MODIS alone, what VIIRS would see in 2020-2025, for 4,188 area-months. Typical (median) error: raw MODIS 75%, one single regional ratio 39%, EmberCal 30%.

Benefits

A consistent 25-year baseline lets responders see the real fire season of their own area, spot unusual months early, and compare the current season with history without being misled by changes of satellite.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, Shapely) for the data pipeline; React, Vite and Leaflet for the web app; hand-made SVG charts; hosted on Vercel. Basemap: Esri World Gray Canvas.

Demo

30-second video: https://embercal.vercel.app/demo/EmberCal-30s.mp4 · 7-slide deck: https://embercal.vercel.app/demo/EmberCal-demo.pdf · Source code: https://github.com/fredericjasmin/embercal
